title: Precision cutline and communication protocol for coordinated API / Console / Runtime release train
creator: Aditi Kapoor
description:
Goal: establish a deterministic, low-friction cut criteria and communication protocol so API, Console, and Runtime releases can ship together while minimizing customer risk and last-minute scope churn.

Scope: this ticket covers milestone definitions, scope-lock gates, automated preflight checks, release-note ownership & templating, cross-team rollback triggers, and a lightweight comms cadence for engineering, design, docs, SRE, and GTM. It does NOT change the runtime deployment mechanics or replace existing canary tooling; it standardizes how we decide what is on the train and how we signal cut decisions.

Success criteria (measurable):
- Every release train has a single canonical cutline document and a scoped list of changes with owners 7 days before the first canary.
- Release notes ownership assigned and draft notes in repo for 90% of user-facing changes 3 days before GA.
- Automated preflight checks (smoke tests, SLO regressions, schema compatibility) run nightly against the train branch with pass/fail signals surfaced to the release board.
- No high-severity post-launch regression attributable to uncoordinated scope changes in last 3 releases.

Deliverables:
1) Cutline matrix template (component, change id, owner, cut-criteria flag, fallback plan).
2) Release-note template in markdown + PR checklist and a small bot that posts reminders to PRs missing release-note metadata.
3) Preflight CI job definitions and dashboards (SLO diffs, integration smoke results, schema-compat).
4) Communication runbook: who to notify at each gate and a one-week preflight cadence (D-7, D-3, D-1).
5) Post-mortem and rollback playbook with automated tag-to-rollback mapping for runtime variants.

Tradeoffs considered: we can be prescriptive (hard locks) or advisory (soft gates). Chosen approach: soft gates with enforced automated checks for critical signals and an accountable escalation path for hard blocks. This reduces last-minute work while allowing urgent security fixes to proceed through an expedited path.
